skippedSources.name: TMAD Flow (Trading Mindset and Data)
skippedSources.reason: Read in full: CPI preview with no data beyond consensus (+0.6% headline, ~0.2% core), plus TMAD app feature announcement; SPX levels section is behind the cut. No analytical content to extract.

items.title: Core CPI 0.3% vs 0.2% expected; energy commodities +35% y/y
items.idea: Sept CPI +0.6% m/m headline (as expected) and +0.3% core vs 0.2% consensus, after +0.4%/+0.3% in Aug. Y/y moved to 3.7% / 2.6% from 3.4% / 2.4%. Energy commodities +9.3% m/m and +35% y/y. CPI ex food, energy and shelter +0.3% for a third month, yet exactly 2.0% y/y.
items.angle: The whole pre-print narrative was 'low bar, Fed pauses, December alive'. A one-tenth core miss tests Oct (22%) vs Dec (86%) hike odds and the 2y. Dauber's short gold/HY book was only wrong on a core of 0.2 or less.
items.tweetA: Core CPI 0.3 vs 0.2. Everyone wrote 'low bar, Fed pauses' this morning. One tenth later, October hike odds sitting at ~22% are the number to watch, not the 0.6 headline. Energy is +35% y/y and the debate is a tenth of a point of core.
items.tweetB: Ex food, energy and shelter: +0.3% three months running, 2.0% y/y. Both facts are true. The 12-month number says target, the 3-month run rate says ~3.6% annualized. Hawks will quote one, doves the other, and the 2-year will decide who wins.

items.title: Beef down 3 months, chicken +1.3%: the CPI basket shows substitution
items.idea: Food at home -0.1% m/m (+1.8% y/y), food away from home +0.2% m/m (+3.5% y/y). Beef down a third straight month; shoppers shifted to chicken, which rose 1.3% in the month. Electricity +0.2% m/m and +4.4% y/y.
items.angle: Real-time demand substitution inside the basket, plus a power price already running 4.4% before the data-center load fully arrives.
items.tweetA: Beef down three months in a row, chicken +1.3% in one. That is what trading down looks like inside a CPI basket, and it shows up while electricity is already +4.4% y/y. Consumers are managing the plate, utilities are managing the grid. $VST $CEG
items.tweetB: Food at home +1.8% y/y, food away +3.5%. The 170bp gap is labor and rent, not wheat. Restaurants carry the inflation, and Domino's just told you customers are cutting items per order.

items.title: Pre-print: core 0.2 would 'lock in an October pause'. It printed 0.3
items.idea: Rosenberg's morning note framed the CPI as the final data before the October FOMC. Consensus was +0.6% headline and +0.2% core (Aug +0.3%). The key was whether energy pass-through reaches non-housing core services and goods or stays in transport and airfares. A 0.2 core 'should be the final data point to lock in an October pause'.
items.angle: The condition he set for the pause was missed by a tenth. Read the breakdown for pass-through into non-housing services before assuming the pause holds.
items.tweetA: Pre-print: a 0.2 core 'locks in an October pause'. Print: 0.3. The pause is now a choice and not a given. Williams already said no to more than one hike, but 'lock in' just became 'probably'.
items.tweetB: The strategist consensus this morning was that the bar is low. The bar was low for the Fed. For anyone long duration with the 10-year at 5.21 it was set the other way. That is the wrong kind of asymmetry.

items.title: Payrolls 29K, wages 3.0%: the Fed is debating hikes into a labor market that stopped hiring
items.idea: FX Daily preview: payrolls were 29K and wage growth 3.0%, the weakest since May 2021. October hike odds fell to ~20% from ~70% pre-payrolls, December still ~72%. Goldman saw core near 0.24% (2.46% y/y) with headline ~0.59%. Core PCE read-through ~0.20%. Core CPI seen ~0.2% in Oct, then ~0.1% in Nov and Dec as shelter cools. All 19 officials backed September's hike.
items.angle: A two-handed Fed: hawkish on December, patient on October, while labor data weakens. The risk case is oil leaking into transport and expectations.
items.tweetA: 29K payrolls and wage growth at 3.0%, the weakest since 2021, and the debate is a December hike. Energy is doing the inflation, labor is doing the opposite. That is stagflation with a policy-error option, not a classic hiking cycle.
items.tweetB: October hike odds went 70% to 20% on one payrolls print, December sits at 72%. The market prices this Fed as fully data-dependent on a 29K number and a 0.3 core at the same time. Pick one. Front-end vol is cheap.

items.title: EUR/USD: the French premium is embedded; 137bp OAT-Bund and rebuilt euro shorts
items.idea: EUR/USD crawled back to ~1.1200 on a softer dollar, not a better euro. France-Germany 10y spread tightened 5bp to 137bp on global bond relief only. Leveraged funds have rebuilt euro shorts; positioning is stretched enough that the next leg lower needs a shove. Firm CPI targets 1.1150-1.1160 with 1.1100 as the tail. 'Cleanest dirty shirt trade.'
items.angle: FX as relative dirt: the dollar's floor is Europe's fiscal stress plus an energy asymmetry.
items.tweetA: OAT-Bund 137bp, tighter by 5bp on a day nothing changed in Paris. That is beta, not repair. EUR/USD at 1.12 is a weaker dollar, not a stronger euro. Dirty shirt trade, still.
items.tweetB: Funds rebuilt euro shorts into 1.12. Hot CPI takes you to 1.1150, a benign print triggers the squeeze. Positioning says the tail is up, macro says down. Size for both.

items.title: Williams: 'rate tweaking cycle'. Market prices Dec at 86% plus two more hikes in 2027
items.idea: NY Fed's Williams: one more hike may be appropriate, no reason to expect more after that, 'not an economy overheating'. Cites disinflationary forces including tariffs, energy and AI. Doves: Williams, Bowman. Hawks: Hammack, Logan. Market: 22% for the meeting in a few weeks, 86% December, and two further hikes in 2027.
items.angle: Gap between a dovish Fed voice and a curve pricing three hikes. One of them is wrong by about 50bp.
items.tweetA: NY Fed's Williams: one more hike, then done. Fed funds futures: December at 86% plus two more in 2027. Someone is wrong by around 50bp and it is the one who doesn't set the policy rate. Or it isn't.
items.tweetB: Williams named AI as a disinflationary force next to fading tariffs. The Fed prices in productivity from the AI boom while the 10-year prices in what it costs to finance it. Both can't clear.

items.title: JPMorgan: card spend +10% y/y 'including gas', investment banking 'slowed a bit'
items.idea: JPM debit and credit spend +10% y/y with momentum across categories including gas and travel. On IB: 'evolving market conditions have recently slowed activity a bit'. Stock down almost 1% Tuesday.
items.angle: Nominal consumer strength with fuel inside it. Cross-check with Citi/WFC provisions and the Domino's basket data.
items.tweetA: JPM: card spend +10% y/y, 'including gas'. With energy commodities +35% y/y in CPI that is a price effect, and the bank calls it demand. Show me the number ex-fuel before I agree.
items.tweetB: JPM says the consumer is fine, IB 'slowed a bit', stock -1%. Citi -5.6% and Wells -3.1% the same day. The market stopped reading banks as a deal story and started reading them as a credit-cost story.

items.title: Rabobank: the move to 5% was the Fed; the move through 5% is term premium
items.idea: Philip Marey (Rabobank) splits the 2026 10-year rise into two phases: to 5% was a Fed-path repricing, through 5% is a term-premium story tied to Treasury vol and public debt. Inflation expectations stayed stable, so real yields did the work. Markets may have overpriced three or four more hikes, but a return below 4.3% is unlikely since the neutral rate and term premium shifted higher. Long rates can ease in 2027 but not back to the pre-Iran-shock regime.
items.angle: A Fed pause doesn't rescue duration if the second leg is a debt premium. Pairs with the 5.21% 10y / 5.56% 30y levels in Dauber's note.
items.tweetA: Two different bond bear markets: 4% to 5% was the Fed, 5% and up is term premium. Breakevens flat, real yields did it. A Fed pause fixes the first one, not the second. The 4.3% floor is gone.
items.tweetB: Inflation expectations stable while nominals rip means the bond market isn't doubting the Fed. It's pricing the Treasury. 10-year at 5.21, 30-year 5.56 on Tuesday. Supply is the tweet, CPI is the noise.

items.title: Goldman: IG credit has a two-month window before AI issuance returns, heavier at the front end
items.idea: IG held up through a bond selloff, renewed Fed hikes, a rate-vol spike and European sovereign stress. Goldman's Jeffrey Papai sees a tactical window into year end because issuance went quiet. Spreads over sovereigns are extraordinarily thin and investors still reach for yield. AI financing is set to return in size, more concentrated at the front of the curve.
items.angle: A temporary supply holiday, not an all-clear. The next test is hundreds of billions of AI paper into the same buyers.
items.tweetA: IG barely moved through a bond selloff, renewed hikes and a vol spike. That isn't resilience, it's a supply holiday. Goldman gives it about two months before AI issuance comes back, front-loaded in the curve.
items.tweetB: Credit has two months. Then hyperscalers need to fund capex with the 10-year above 5%. Dauber says private credit is already gated at ~40% redemption requests. AI financing is a marginal-buyer problem across both public and private.

items.title: Private credit: 73% of LBOs priced under S+500 vs 9% in 2020; Blue Owl tech fund redemptions ~40%
items.idea: 73% of 2026 private-credit LBO financings priced under 500bp over SOFR vs 9% in 2020; share over 700bp fell to 2% from 23%. Private credit yield 9.1% vs 8.6% for leveraged loans, so the premium that once exceeded 2 points is near nothing. Blue Owl's tech lending fund saw redemption requests of 40.7%, 38.1% and 39.0% in three quarters against caps near 5%. HY printed 311bp on Oct 12 while CCC sat at 1,252bp, a fresh cycle wide. He's short premium BDCs; wrong if HY near 290bp with the 10y above 5.00.
items.angle: Gate math plus tail-spread evidence. Stress is parked where the index can't see it.
items.tweetA: 73% of 2026 private-credit LBOs priced under S+500, vs 9% in 2020. Premium over loans: about 50bp for giving up the exit. Blue Owl's tech fund has had ~40% redemption requests three quarters running against ~5% caps. At that cap, clearing 40% takes eight quarters with no new requests.
items.tweetB: HY at 311bp, CCC at 1,252bp, a cycle wide. The index says calm, the tail says triage. The stress isn't in the spread you watch, it's in the one you can't mark.

items.title: S&P 0.2% from the high, median stock 15% off; 224 sessions without an 80% down-volume day
items.idea: S&P closed Tuesday 0.2% under its record while the median stock is 15% under its own high. Fund managers are most overweight tech since Aug 2020 and most underweight consumer discretionary since 2008. NYSE has gone 224 sessions without an 80% downside-volume day, the longest run since at least 1996.
items.angle: Narrow-leadership market with extreme consensus: long tech, short consumer.
items.tweetA: S&P 0.2% from the high. Median stock 15% below its own. 224 sessions without an 80% down-volume day, the longest since at least 1996. FMs most long tech since Aug 2020. It is a one-factor market wearing an index costume.
items.tweetB: Fund managers: most underweight consumer discretionary since 2008. Domino's just cut guidance on shrinking baskets and JetBlue is down seven straight. They are right on the consumer and crowded on tech. That is a pair trade, not a view.

items.title: ASML guides Q4 to EUR14.7B vs 14.0B; Micron -3.6%, AMAT -6.7% on CXMT's denser DRAM cell
items.idea: ASML guided Q4 sales to a EUR14.7B midpoint vs EUR14.0B expected; customers are asking to place orders for 2029 and 2030; EPS EUR12.93 vs 10.71, op margin 44.4% vs 41.8%, capacity review beyond the 30% already planned for 2028. Same tape: Micron -3.6% (sixth straight decline for US chipmakers) and Applied Materials -6.7% on CXMT's cell architecture and a patent exclusion filing. Dauber: 'the machines sell, the chips they make get cheaper'. Short Micron; wrong if Kospi > 6,300 on foreign buying.
items.angle: Cost-curve read: tool demand up, memory pricing down. TSMC Thursday is the next test (Q4 capex ~$20B on the street).
items.tweetA: ASML guides Q4 to EUR14.7B vs 14.0B and customers are booking 2029-2030. Micron -3.6% and AMAT -6.7% the same day on a Chinese DRAM cell. The toolmaker sells to everyone, the memory maker eats the price deflation. $ASML $MU
items.tweetB: CXMT's denser cell plus ASML adding capacity beyond the 30% already planned for 2028 equals a DRAM supply wave in the schedule. Memory ran 5x on scarcity. Scarcity ends when your customer's customer builds fabs.

items.title: Houthi strike hits Aramco's Dhahran office; Houthis building 1,200-mile missiles with Chinese parts
items.idea: A Houthi strike started a 'limited fire' at an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran late Tuesday; intercepts over Riyadh and two other Saudi sites. The Houthis are assembling a version of Iran's Kheibar Shekan with Chinese-supplied parts, ~1,200 miles of range (WSJ / Conflict Armament Research), covering all of Saudi Arabia and Israel. IEA: Gulf crude exports near pre-war levels; Saudi output +2mb/d in September. Brent $106.55. He owns the premium via freight and a small call spread.
items.angle: Brent is a premium on infrastructure risk, not lost barrels. Option-like, not supply-like.
items.tweetA: Houthis hit an Aramco building in Dhahran and are building 1,200-mile missiles from Chinese parts. The IEA says Gulf exports are near pre-war levels. So Brent at $106 is a premium on infrastructure risk, not lost barrels. That trades like an option, not like supply.
items.tweetB: 1,200 miles covers all of Saudi Arabia and Israel, with Iranian design and Chinese parts. The chokepoint is components, not launchers. Watch for export-control and component-sanction headlines aimed at Chinese electronics suppliers.

items.title: Iran says it wants oil above $100 into the midterms; 'energy ceasefire' Moscow hadn't heard of
items.idea: Iran is hitting tankers around Hormuz to keep oil above $100 into US midterms, and its officials say so on the record. The White House announced an 'energy ceasefire' in Ukraine that Moscow appears not to know about and cut a diesel deal with Putin three weeks before an election. Russia answered by hitting Kyiv's power plants.
items.angle: Energy price is now an explicit political weapon in a US election cycle, from both sides.
items.tweetA: Iran says openly it wants oil above $100 until the midterms. Trump cuts a diesel deal with Putin three weeks out. Energy price is now the declared weapon in a US election.
items.tweetB: Moscow answered the 'energy ceasefire' by hitting Kyiv's power plants. Each side thought it bought something different. Trade the headline, not the treaty.

items.title: China Sept exports +36.3% y/y vs 25.7% expected on AI hardware; PPI +5.0%
items.idea: Overnight China September trade: exports +36.3% y/y vs 25.7% expected, driven by AI hardware; PPI +5.0% y/y. Dauber (citing FT): the record surplus is the other side of the capex boom.
items.angle: US hyperscaler capex shows up as Chinese export strength and producer pricing power. Pair with the CXMT item.
items.tweetA: China exports +36.3% y/y vs 25.7% expected, PPI +5%. The US capex boom is China's trade surplus. Both are being booked in the same quarter that Europe narrows its supply-chain rules.
items.tweetB: PPI +5% is pricing power, not deflation. A US hyperscaler is the marginal buyer of Chinese hardware, so the AI boom has a Chinese cost-of-goods line. Not the Chinese consumer paying.

items.title: Diesel of Discontent: 136 of 140 Yamal LNG cargoes went to Europe in H1 (~$7B)
items.idea: H1 2026: of 140 ships leaving Russia's Yamal LNG, 136 offloaded in Europe, mainly France, Belgium, Spain, Netherlands, worth about $7B to Moscow. In May the UK carved a sanctions exception for Russian crude refined in India despite the outcry. EU ministers reiterate 'pressure on Russia' after Trump's diesel deal. Doomberg: the West's economic war on Russia was flawed from the start, there is a better way.
items.angle: Sanctions hypocrisy as policy risk: the next exemption comes when pump prices bite.
items.tweetA: 136 of 140 Yamal LNG cargoes went to Europe in H1, ~$7B to Moscow. Same ministers now condemning Trump's diesel deal. Energy sanctions have always been 'for thee'. The next exception arrives when a pump price does.
items.tweetB: Doomberg's argument is that sanctions hurt Europe's cost curve more than Russia's. The tradeable version: European diesel is priced by politics, not refinery capacity. $VLO $MPC $TTE

items.title: Strive outbought Strategy 13-to-1: 3,311 BTC ($280M) vs 250 BTC; Strategy mNAV below 1.0
items.idea: Strive bought 3,311 BTC for ~$280M between Oct 5 and 9 at ~$84.5k average, its biggest buy since January (32,773 BTC, ~$2.73B). Strategy bought 250 BTC for $21.5M, and spent $192M buying back its own preferreds that week. Strategy's mNAV fell below 1.0 for the first time. Strategy still holds 848,250 BTC (newsletter says ~$51B, but at $83.4k that is ~$70.7B, so $51B looks like cost basis).
items.angle: Biggest holder and most aggressive buyer are now different entities. Strategy trades under its coins.
items.tweetA: Strive bought 3,311 BTC last week. Strategy bought 250 and spent $192M buying back its own preferred. The machine that bought every dip is now buying its own paper. Different engine, different regime.
items.tweetB: Strategy's mNAV is below 1.0, so the market values the company at less than its 848,250 BTC. (At $83.4k that's ~$70B, not the $51B in the note; that's cost basis.) When the biggest treasury trades at a discount, the question becomes who liquidates, not who buys.

items.title: Strive sells $500M of 15% daily-pay preferred to buy BTC; STRC at $99.90 near par
items.idea: Strive is selling 5M shares of a new preferred at $100 for $500M with a fixed 15% dividend paid daily, proceeds to Bitcoin. That is $75M a year in coupon. STRC (Strategy's preferred) hit $99.90, the highest since the May depeg; at $100 par Strategy's issuance faucet turns on.
items.angle: BTC treasuries as leveraged yield products: the asset must beat 15% just to break even for common holders.
items.tweetA: Strive: $500M of preferred at 15%, paid daily. That's $75M a year to buy an asset that yields zero. BTC has to compound over 15% just for the common to break even. The largest buyer is also the most expensive borrower.
items.tweetB: STRC at $99.90, a hair under par, which is where Strategy's issuance machine restarts. Daily-pay preferreds on both sides: BTC treasuries are turning into money-market funds that buy bitcoin.

items.title: Dormant 4,582 BTC wallet splits into five addresses as ETFs take in $175M
items.idea: A wallet that held through every crash since 2020 moved its full 4,581.94 BTC (~$377M) on Oct 12 across five new addresses. BTC ETFs: +$175M net inflows Tuesday; ETH ETFs: +$25M, ending a 10-day outflow streak. BTC $83.4k, ETH $2,500, SOL $107, gold -0.4% at $4,160, oil +4% at $96.
items.angle: Whale movement isn't a sale, but exchange deposits would tell. ETF streak ending is a lack of sellers, not yet demand.
items.tweetA: A wallet that held through every drawdown since 2020 moved all 4,581.94 BTC into five addresses on the same day ETFs took in $175M. Moving isn't selling, but it's how selling starts. Watch exchange deposits.
items.tweetB: ETH ETFs broke a 10-day outflow streak with $25M. A streak ending at $25M is no bottom, it's a lack of sellers. ETH at $2,500 needs real bids.

items.title: Ledger supply-chain implants: MediaMarkt Saturn pulls Ledger; Trezor cuts reseller channel
items.idea: MediaMarkt Saturn stopped selling Ledger hardware wallets as of Oct 13 after a German customer reported an implant (no loss in that case). Ledger asked resellers in Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Hong Kong to suspend sales; confirmed incidents are in Southeast Asia, no sign Ledger's own infrastructure was compromised. Probe began Oct 9 with reseller CryptoBilis. Trezor is narrowing resellers (Lucky Trader says all authorizations end Jan 1, 2027).
items.angle: Self-custody's weak point is the box in the middle of the supply chain, not the seed math.
items.tweetA: MediaMarkt pulls Ledger, Southeast Asian resellers are suspended, and Ledger says its own systems weren't breached. The attack is in the cardboard. Hardware-wallet security assumes the box wasn't touched.
items.tweetB: Trezor's response is to cut resellers. Direct-to-consumer only becomes the standard, which hands Ledger and Trezor pricing power while killing retail distribution. Self-custody is going vertical.

items.title: Coinbase (~5% of all BTC) hands devs a quantum wish list shaped by custody
items.idea: Coinbase, which says it holds ~5% of all BTC, asks for an output type that lets new post-quantum signature schemes be swapped in later, a 1-of-2 hybrid key spendable with classical or PQ key, and a stateless fallback if stateful schemes are adopted. Its signing servers run independently across zones, which a scheme requiring an exclusive lock per key would break. Legacy, dormant and lost coins are 'a separate governance and engineering problem'.
items.angle: Post-quantum BTC may be decided by an operational constraint at one custodian. Dormant coins question deferred.
items.tweetA: Coinbase holds ~5% of all BTC and told developers the quantum upgrade has to work for custodians: swap-in signature types, 1-of-2 hybrid keys, a stateless fallback. A custodian with 5% of supply now has a seat at the BIP table.
items.tweetB: Their signers run independently across zones, so any scheme needing an exclusive lock per key is a non-starter. Quantum-safe Bitcoin may hinge on one operational constraint at one exchange. And 'dormant coins' is the Satoshi question, deferred again.

items.title: Sui ships first native quantum-safe tx on devnet; mainnet auth targeted Q1 2027
items.idea: Sui processed its first native quantum-safe transaction on devnet (Mysten Labs added ML-DSA-65 in v1.82.0), targeting testnet accounts by year-end and mainnet authentication in Q1 2027. Coinbase backs BIP-360 (P2MR) and P2TRv2 for Bitcoin, with a phased rollout where active wallets can spend with old or quantum-safe keys.
items.angle: Narrative gap: young chains ship PQ in quarters; Bitcoin governs it over years.
items.tweetA: Sui ran its first native quantum-safe transaction on devnet, mainnet authentication in Q1 2027. Bitcoin is still debating which output type to use. Fast chains can ship PQ in quarters, the largest asset needs years of governance. That gap is a tradeable narrative.
items.tweetB: Bitcoin is the slowest-moving L1 by design, which is a feature until someone puts a credible quantum date on the calendar. Then it's a risk premium, and Sui-style chains get a marketing line.

items.title: Solana Alpenglow goes live on mainnet Oct 21: finality from ~12.8s to ~150ms
items.idea: Anza set Oct 21 for mainnet-beta activation of Alpenglow, replacing TowerBFT with Votor, cutting finality from ~12.8 seconds to ~150 milliseconds and moving validator votes off-chain. Testnet and devnet migrations are done. SOL +1% at $107.
items.angle: Event risk on the upgrade itself. Sub-second finality changes what can run on-chain: order books, payments, agents.
items.tweetA: Solana finality goes from ~12.8s to ~150ms on Oct 21, votes moved off-chain. Sub-second finality changes what can run on-chain. SOL at $107 is pricing none of it, and the risk is in the migration itself.
items.tweetB: Legacy settlement is T+1. Solana would be ~150ms. Compare with BNY and Citadel needing 'minutes' for a tokenized Treasury repo. The product is the gap between how fast it can settle and how fast the plumbing lets it.

items.title: BNY and Citadel settle a tokenized Treasury triparty repo in minutes; IBKR turns on ETH staking
items.idea: BNY completed a tokenized U.S. Treasury triparty repo workflow with Citadel Securities, the first use of tokenized assets on the platform: the tokenized note settled within minutes and was used as collateral in an overnight repo. Interactive Brokers added ether staking via zerohash, rewards paid as additional staked ETH that compounds.
items.angle: TradFi's use of chains is collateral mobility, not tokens as an asset class.
items.tweetA: BNY and Citadel settled a tokenized Treasury in minutes and used it as overnight repo collateral. The point isn't 24/7 trading, it's recycling cash faster. That's TradFi's version of blockchains, and nobody mentions the token.
items.tweetB: IBKR staking ETH via zerohash, rewards compounding in-kind. Brokers are becoming yield distributors. The ETF staking debate was a side show, the broker rail is the product.

items.title: Sberbank joins both of Russia's crypto registers; first products Dec 1
items.idea: Bank of Russia added Sberbank to its register of crypto exchange operators on Oct 12, six days after it reportedly landed among the first digital depositories. Four firms (VTB, T-Invest Lab, Zefir, Sistema-Crypto) were added Oct 6; Interfax counts eight organizations besides Sberbank, the central bank's own records at least nine. Sberbank aims to roll out first crypto products Dec 1.
items.angle: Russia is building a licensed crypto rail at speed while sanctions deny SWIFT access.
items.tweetA: Sberbank is now on both of Russia's new crypto registers, with products due Dec 1. VTB and three others were licensed six days earlier. The Russian state is building a regulated crypto rail in weeks.
items.tweetB: A state that can't use SWIFT is the most motivated adopter of a rail that doesn't need it. Licensed exchange operators plus bank depositories is how cross-border settlement gets built without announcing it as such.

items.title: UK court: Chinese law governs victims' claims on 61,000 seized BTC (~$5B)
items.idea: UK High Court ruled Chinese law governs fraud victims' claims to 61,000 bitcoin (~$5B) seized in the Zhimin Qian case, making recovery harder for victims and improving the government's chance of keeping the coins. Victims' lawyers are appealing; a further hearing decides whether any victims have a claim.
items.angle: A sovereign overhang or holding: 61k BTC is nearly twice Strive's stack.
items.tweetA: UK High Court: Chinese law governs victims' claims on 61,000 seized BTC, about $5B. Choice of law decided a $5B question. The government's odds of keeping the coins just went up.
items.tweetB: 61,000 BTC is nearly twice Strive's 32,773. The UK could become one of the larger BTC holders without a mNAV, a strategy or a view. Whether it holds or sells is a supply-side overhang.

items.title: South Korea to block 27 unregistered exchanges; Philippines' Coins.ph reportedly faces central-bank action
items.idea: South Korea will block domestic access to 27 unregistered exchanges, including Bitmart and KuCoin, extending earlier app blocks by Google and Apple; operators face up to 5 years. Coins.ph, the Philippines' largest exchange, reportedly faces central bank action over alleged service to offshore gambling firms (denied).
items.angle: Asian regulators are enforcing through app stores and network layers, not exchanges.
items.tweetA: South Korea is blocking 27 unregistered exchanges and the Philippines is reportedly circling Coins.ph. Asia is closing offshore on-ramps while Russia licenses its own.
items.tweetB: Enforcement moved from the exchange to the pipe: app stores, ISPs. Regulators no longer need the exchange's cooperation. Watch offshore volume share in Asia.

items.title: Binance closes Binance Pool and Cloud Mining; ~2.3% of hashrate has 28 days to move
items.idea: Binance is closing Binance Pool and Cloud Mining; connections cut 7am UTC Nov 10, giving miners 28 days. Per Lucky Trader it exits mining after nine years with roughly 2.3% of network hashrate. Also: Ripple and Stripe-owned Privy partner to bring embedded wallets to XRPL, including for x402 agent payments; Tether seeds EFY Finance for institutional stablecoin use in 17 LatAm countries.
items.angle: Pool-concentration relief, a hashrate migration on Nov 10, and agent-payments plumbing.
items.tweetA: Binance exits mining after nine years: ~2.3% of hashrate has 28 days to find a new pool. Watch Foundry and Antpool share after Nov 10.
items.tweetB: Ripple and Stripe-owned Privy are putting programmable wallets on XRPL for x402 payments by software agents. Tether seeds LatAm stablecoin settlement in 17 countries. Rails for agent money are being carved up before agents transact at scale.

items.title: Robinhood Chain DEX volume -61% in five weeks; Standard's launchpad needs $1B volume per $1M fees
items.idea: Average daily DEX volume on Robinhood Chain fell from $2.29B (Sep 1-15) to $897M (Oct 6-12), about -61%. Standard's launchpad ('King of the Markets') launches with a 1M+ USDG rewards pool. At a 0.10% retained fee, $1M of fees needs $1B of volume; at 0.05% it needs $2B. Standard's pool holds ~$15.8M (2,600 ETH + 28.8M STANDARD) vs ~$26M market cap; 970 Charters, 3,468 Branches, 0.35x issuance = 245,000 STANDARD/day (~71 per Branch). Author's retention test: volume at least half of final campaign week four weeks after.
items.angle: Incentive-led volume on a chain that lost most of its volume. Tokenized stocks lack equity rights (AMC CEO argument).

items.tweetB: The author says 70-80% of his agent's capability comes from its knowing him. Memory is the lock-in, not the model. Which makes the 'who is allowed to access my data' fights (Amazon vs Meta's Muse) the real contest.

items.title: AI builders privately war-gaming the public revolt after the first catastrophic AI event (Axios)

items.angle: Regulatory tail risk with a 'when' rather than an 'if', unpriced in AI multiples.

items.title: Claude designed binders for 15 targets; Twist tested 1,260 designs in under three weeks, 14 of 15 confirmed

items.title: AI-discovered molecules pass Phase I 80-90% vs 40-65%, but Phase II ~40%: same as industry
items.idea: Average new drug costs ~$2.7B and 100+ months of clinical trials (Deloitte, 2025). BCG (Drug Discovery Today 2024): AI-discovered molecules advance through Phase I 80-90% vs 40-65% historically, but Phase II success ~40%, near industry average. No AI-discovered drug is approved; Insilico's rentosertib entered Phase III in July 2026. Isomorphic's first clinical trials slipped to late 2026. Mass General Brigham JAMA trial: AI patient screening gave 35 vs 19 enrolments (4,476 patients).
items.angle: AI helps find molecules that behave, not molecules that work. Efficacy is still the wall.
items.tweetA: AI-discovered molecules clear Phase I 80-90% of the time vs 40-65% historically. Phase II: ~40%, the industry average. Models find molecules that behave, not molecules that work. A $2.7B drug doesn't get cheaper until Phase II does.
items.tweetB: No AI-discovered drug is approved yet. The furthest, rentosertib, entered Phase III in July, and Isomorphic's first trials slipped a year. Biotech is the cleanest test of how fast 'AI revolution' timelines should be discounted.

items.title: Sweden MASAI: AI mammography found 29% more cancers with 44% less reading workload
items.idea: MASAI trial (~106,000 women, Lancet Jan 2026): AI-supported mammography detected 29% more cancers, cut radiologists' screen-reading workload by 44% and reduced interval cancers by 12%. AMA March 2026: 81% of US physicians use AI vs 38% in 2023. FDA's AI device list hit 1,614 by end of June 2026, ~three-quarters radiology (GE HealthCare 134, Siemens Healthineers 101, Philips 62). A JAMA study found AI scribes save 16 minutes of charting a day and ~$167 a month per clinician; Epic bundles scribes and Doximity gives one away.
items.angle: Clean productivity result in radiology vs commoditized scribes. Value accrues to workflow owners.
items.tweetA: Sweden's 106,000-woman trial: AI mammography found 29% more cancers, cut reading workload 44%, and interval cancers fell 12%. More output, less labor, better outcome. It's the cleanest AI productivity result I've seen in any field.
items.tweetB: 81% of US doctors use AI, but scribes save 16 minutes a day and ~$167 a month per clinician, and Epic bundles them while Doximity gives one away. The most-adopted AI product has no pricing power. The gain goes to the hospital. $DOCS $GEHC

items.title: 107 fired Chinese graduates got 30 minutes to decide (law: 30 days) and complained up the supply chain
items.idea: Xingyu Automotive Lighting (supplier to BMW, VW, Mercedes, Audi; preparing a Hong Kong IPO) laid off 107 graduates after one month, offering half a month's pay or factory-floor jobs, a third hold master's degrees. Law requires 30 days' notice, they got 30 minutes. 'Fresh graduate' status (about 70% of national civil-service posts, some hukou benefits) is single-use, and factory floor experience cuts offers 10-30%. They recorded the meetings and complained to Mercedes, VW, BMW and HKEX. A background check with litigation records costs 195 yuan (~$30). Mercedes cited 'serious ethical misconduct' and VW opened a special investigation.
items.angle: Youth white-collar precarity with a new lever: foreign customers' compliance channels.
items.tweetA: 107 laid-off Chinese graduates were given 30 minutes to decide when the law requires 30 days. They recorded the meeting, then complained to BMW, VW and Mercedes during Xingyu's IPO prep. Supply-chain due diligence became labor enforcement from abroad.
items.tweetB: 'Fresh graduate' status is single-use: ~70% of national civil-service posts are reserved for it, and one month on payroll burns it. A one-time credential, a 195-yuan market for your litigation history, and a graduate cohort with no leverage. That's the pressure cooker in a flagging economy.

items.title: EU Omnibus I lifted the CSDDD threshold to 5,000 employees / EUR1.5B just as it became a labor lever
items.idea: The EU's Omnibus I (Feb 24, 2026) raised CSDDD coverage from >1,000 employees and EUR450M turnover to >5,000 employees and EUR1.5B, with more flexibility on which risks to investigate. The Merz government proposes dropping LkSG reporting requirements and limiting fines to serious violations. In China a Sept 1 article called for legislation treating 'complaining to foreigners' (告洋状) like organized crime, then was deleted. Xingyu chair's punishment was a 12-month salary cut.
items.angle: Deregulation narrows supply-chain leverage at the same moment workers learn to use it; Beijing frames complaints as foreign weapons.
items.tweetA: The EU raised the CSDDD threshold from 1,000 employees/EUR450M to 5,000/EUR1.5B in February. The tool Chinese workers used against Xingyu now covers far fewer suppliers. Deregulation and supply-chain leverage are moving in opposite directions.
items.tweetB: In China, an op-ed demanded 'complaining to foreigners' be treated like organized crime before it was deleted. Europe narrows its rules while Beijing calls compliance complaints foreign weapons. Supply-chain due diligence is a geopolitical battlefield. $BMW $VOW3 $MBG

items.title: GitLab -7.3%: max-severity unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2026-97229) in the CI/CD regex compiler
items.idea: GitLab disclosed and patched CVE-2026-97229, a maximum-severity flaw in self-managed CE/EE that lets unauthenticated attackers execute code through a crafted CI/CD configuration; the issue is in the CI/CD regex compiler. items.angle: Pipeline config as attack surface: source, credentials, deploy infrastructure.
items.tweetA: GitLab -7.25% on a max-severity unauthenticated RCE through a crafted CI/CD config. The attack surface is the pipeline itself: source, deploy credentials, infra. Software-supply-chain risk is software-factory risk. $GTLB
items.tweetB: GitLab.com and Dedicated were patched already; only self-managed customers are exposed. Every maximum-severity CVE is a migration pitch to hosted. The cloud vs self-hosted gap is a security product in itself.
